title: Three Ways a Building Fails Before It Is Finished
summary: Construction failures that reach the news usually start as one of three quiet events: a design change after sign-off, a hold point that was bypassed, or a contractor whose finances were failing in plain sight. Ford teaches the common root, a control that exists on paper and is allowed to be skipped, and how an owner keeps each one working.
body:
Most construction disasters begin as an ordinary shortcut through a control that already existed: a change that skipped its engineer, an inspection that was waved through, or a contractor's cash problem that everyone could see and no one priced.

Recall

Q. What is a building's code basis?

A. The occupancy classification, construction type, sprinkler status, allowable height and area and fire-resistance ratings on which its approval rests, judged under the code edition in force when the permit was filed.

Q. What is the difference between functional testing and integrated systems testing in commissioning?

A. Functional testing proves each system works on its own as designed. Integrated testing proves the systems work together, for example that a fire alarm signal correctly triggers smoke control, elevator recall and door release.

Q. What is a pre-pour checklist?

A. A signed check, before concrete is placed, that formwork, reinforcement, embedded items, cover, inspections and the concrete order are all correct, because after the pour most errors can only be fixed by demolition.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the fourth post-mortem week. We have studied finance failures, legal and partnership failures and wealth failures. Now we study the building itself. I want you to leave this week with one idea above all: you will almost never be undone by a problem nobody had a control for. You will be undone by a control that existed and was skipped, by people who were each acting reasonably, under schedule pressure, on your project.

Failure mode one: the change after sign-off

Plain English first. At some point the design is signed off: the engineer has approved it, the authority has permitted it and the contractor has priced it. After that point, any change, however small it looks, can travel through the building in ways only the designer understands. A change after sign-off that does not go back to the engineer of record is a change nobody has checked.

The professional framing is change control: a written route by which any change to an approved design, including a substitution proposed in a shop drawing, the contractor's detailed drawing of how a component will be made, is reviewed by the designer responsible for it before it is built. The best-known example is the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City. On July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways collapsed into a crowded atrium and 114 people were killed. A connection designed as a single continuous hanger rod was changed during shop drawing preparation to two offset rods, which roughly doubled the load on one connection. The change was not properly checked before it was built.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A contractor proposes substituting a cheaper anchor for the specified one on a heavy facade bracket, saving 40,000 dollars. Routed properly, the engineer's review costs about 3,000 dollars and two weeks. Routed through a site meeting, it costs nothing until a bracket fails. The owner's job is not to judge the anchor. It is to make sure no substitution reaches site without the responsible designer's written approval.

Failure mode two: the bypassed hold point

A hold point is a step in the work beyond which the contractor may not proceed until a named inspection has been done and released in writing. A witness point is gentler: the inspector must be notified and may attend, but the work can proceed if they do not come. Reinforcement inspection before a pour, a waterproofing inspection before backfill and a fire-stopping inspection before a ceiling closes are classic hold points, because the work about to cover them makes them invisible.

Worked example two, hypothetical. The reinforcement inspection on a transfer slab is booked for 7 in the morning. The inspector is delayed until 11, and the concrete trucks are already ordered. The site pours at 8. The inspection is now impossible. To verify the slab afterwards, the engineer requires a scan of the reinforcement and some cores, costing perhaps 25,000 dollars and a week, and if anything is wrong, the remedy may be demolition. The trucks could have been held at a cost of a few thousand dollars in standby charges. A bypassed hold point converts a small, certain cost into a large, uncertain one.

Say that out loud now.

A hold point is released in writing, by name, before the work covers it. No release, no pour.

Failure mode three: the contractor who is failing in plain sight

Contractors fail like any business, and large ones fail too. Carillion, one of the largest construction and services contractors in the United Kingdom, went into compulsory liquidation on January 15, 2018, leaving public hospital projects among others unfinished. Ford's Day 2 lesson takes that case apart. The first principle here is that a contractor's collapse is rarely a surprise to the people closest to it. The signs are cash signs: subcontractors paid late, extended payment terms, revenue resting on claims not yet agreed, a request to reduce retainage, a sudden wish to bill ahead of work.

The professional framing is counterparty monitoring: treating the contractor's financial health as a project risk with its own owner, indicators and triggers, rather than as something checked once at prequalification.

The common root

Put the three side by side and the pattern is the same. A control existed: change review, the hold point, the payment and prequalification process. Under pressure, someone treated it as optional. Each individual decision was defensible in the moment. The owner's role is to make the controls non-negotiable before the pressure arrives, because once the trucks are at the gate, nobody wants to be the person who says stop.

Three tools do most of that work, and none of them is expensive. First, a written list, agreed with the contractor at the start, of every hold point and every category of change that must return to a designer. Second, a named person, by role, who may release each item, so that nobody on site can claim the authority by being the most senior person present. Third, a standing instruction, written into the contract and repeated at the first site meeting, that the owner will pay standby costs for waiting on a release but will not pay for work built without one. The third tool changes the economics on the morning it matters: waiting becomes cheap and skipping becomes expensive.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: rework and demolition costs may be treated differently from original construction for tax purposes, and recoveries from a contractor or surety have their own character; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: an owner who directs a change or a pour can share liability for what follows. Banking: lenders and their monitors watch hold point records and contractor payment practice, and a failure in either can stop draws. Governance: name in writing who may release a hold point and who may approve a change. Estate: a latent defect can surface years later, long after the people who made the decision have gone; your records are what protect your successors. Exit: buyers and their engineers ask for inspection records, and a building with gaps in them sells at a discount, if it sells.

Professional sign-off required: engineer of record, on every change to the structure; special inspector or testing agency, on every hold point release.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that the controls are written in the specification and owned by nobody on site. The control is an owner's hold point register and change log, reviewed weekly, with a named person who may release each item and a standing instruction that nothing proceeds without that release.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that because an inspection was booked, it happened, or that because a shop drawing was stamped "reviewed", the engineer approved the change. Ask for the release and read the stamp.

Callback

In Week 116, Ingrid taught inspection and test plans, hold and witness points and nonconformance reports as the backbone of a quality plan. This week shows what happens when that backbone is treated as paperwork. The plan only works if someone with authority enforces it on the morning it is inconvenient.

Recap

Three failure modes: a change after sign-off that skipped its engineer, a hold point bypassed under schedule pressure, and a contractor failing in plain sight. One root: a control that existed and was allowed to be skipped. Make each control non-negotiable before the pressure arrives.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Carillion, 2018, seen from the owner's side of the contract.
checklist: I keep an owner's hold point register with a named releaser for each item.
I require written release of every hold point before the work covers it.
I route every substitution and change after sign-off to the responsible designer in writing.
I read the review stamp on shop drawings and know what it does and does not approve.
I hold concrete trucks rather than pour without a released inspection.
I monitor the contractor's payment of subcontractors every month.
I treat requests to reduce retainage or bill ahead as financial warning signs.
I review the change log and hold point register every week.
head: Field checklist
speak: Most construction failures start as a shortcut through a control that already existed. There are three common ones. First, a change after sign-off that never went back to the engineer of record; at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City in 1981, a hanger rod detail changed during shop drawings roughly doubled the load on one connection, and the walkways collapsed, killing 114 people. Second, a bypassed hold point: an inspection that must be released in writing before work covers it, waved through because the trucks were already ordered. Third, a contractor failing in plain sight, with late payments to subcontractors and revenue resting on unagreed claims, as Carillion did before its liquidation in 2018. The common root is a control treated as optional under pressure. The owner's job is to make those controls non-negotiable, with named releasers and a weekly register, before the pressure arrives.
terms: Hold point — a stage in the work beyond which the contractor may not proceed until a named inspection is done and released in writing.
Witness point — a stage at which the inspector must be notified and may attend, but work may proceed if they do not.
Change control — the written process by which any change to an approved design is reviewed by the responsible designer before it is built.

hostile.q: Your site poured a transfer slab before the reinforcement inspection. Why should I keep funding this project?
hostile.a: Because we caught it and stopped, and I can show you exactly what we are doing about it. The pour happened without the released inspection; that broke our procedure and I have named who authorised it. The engineer of record has specified a reinforcement scan and cores, which are under way and costed. Until the engineer accepts the slab in writing, no load goes on it and no further pour proceeds without a written release from the named inspector. I will send you the engineer's report the day it arrives, whatever it says.

title: Carillion 2018: The Contractor Everyone Thought Was Too Big to Fail
summary: Ford, with Roman, takes the collapse of Carillion in January 2018 through seven forensic steps, from the owner's side of the contract. The lesson is that size is not solvency, and that the signs of a contractor's failure are usually visible in how it pays its supply chain long before it stops.
body:
Carillion was one of the largest contractors in its country, and it failed anyway; the owners left with unfinished buildings were the ones who mistook its size for evidence that it could pay its way.

Recall

Q. In reverse engineering a building, why do you plan on the average floor cycle rather than the best?

A. Because the best floor shows what the system could do; the average shows what the project actually did once weather, breakdowns, inspections and the learning curve are included.

Q. What is a latent defect?

A. A defect that was not discoverable by reasonable inspection at completion and appears later. How long an owner can claim for it depends on the contract and the limitation law.

Q. What is reshoring?

A. Placing temporary supports back under a slab after its formwork is stripped, so that it can share the load of fresh slabs above before it reaches full strength.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this failure was told in money long before it was told in unfinished buildings. You will never hire a contractor of Carillion's size. That is precisely why the case matters: if the signs were visible at that scale, they will be visible at yours, and smaller contractors fail faster. I will keep to facts I am confident of and avoid figures I cannot confirm.

1. Timeline

Carillion was a large British construction and facilities services group with public and private clients, including hospitals built under long-term public-private contracts. In July 2017 it issued a profit warning, a public statement that results would fall well short of expectations, driven by large write-downs on a number of construction contracts. Its share price fell sharply. Further warnings followed in the autumn. On January 15, 2018, after talks with lenders and the government failed, the company entered compulsory liquidation, a court-ordered winding up. Public services it ran were taken over, and construction projects, including two large hospitals, the Royal Liverpool University Hospital and the Midland Metropolitan hospital, were left to be completed by others, years late. A parliamentary inquiry reported in May 2018 and criticised the company's directors and its auditors.

2. Key decisions

From the owner's side, three decisions mattered. Awarding large, complex contracts to the lowest or most confident bid. Relying on the contractor's scale as a proxy for security, with protections sized for a normal contractor default rather than a total one. And, as warnings accumulated in 2017, continuing to deal with the contractor as if the risk were someone else's to manage.

3. Assumptions

The central assumption was that a firm so large, with so many government contracts, could not simply stop. The inquiry's account suggests the company itself was booking revenue on contracts on the expectation of recovering disputed sums and of future margins that did not arrive. Owners assumed that what the contractor reported about a project's financial position was close to the truth. On a contract in difficulty, the contractor's view and the owner's view of value diverge, and only one of them is under the owner's control.

4. Incentives

A contractor bidding to win work has an incentive to price optimistically and recover through claims. A listed company has an incentive to report steady profits and maintain dividends. Owners had an incentive to accept the lowest compliant price. Subcontractors had little power to resist long payment terms. Each incentive was rational. Together they pushed risk down the supply chain and forward in time, where it accumulated unseen.

Say that out loud now.

Size is not solvency. A contractor's health shows first in how it pays the people below it.

5. Warning signs ignored

Reported in the inquiry and the press: long payment terms imposed on subcontractors, said to have stretched to about 120 days [unverified — confirm independently], with an early-payment financing scheme through which suppliers could be paid sooner at a discount. Heavy reliance on contract revenue not yet agreed with clients. A large pension deficit. Dividends maintained while debt rose. At project level, owners see versions of these signs: subcontractors complaining of late payment, a contractor pushing hard on disputed variations, slower progress with fewer workers on site, and requests to accelerate payments. Each is a cash signal.

6. Point of no return

For the company, the point of no return came between the profit warning in July 2017 and the failed rescue talks in January 2018. For an owner, it came earlier: the last date at which the owner could still have prepared for a default, by securing the supply chain, checking bond and guarantee positions, documenting the state of the work and planning a step-in, while the contractor was still functioning. After the liquidation, every owner was negotiating from a stopped site.

Notice what an owner could still have done in the autumn of 2017, on any contract with such a counterparty. Photograph and measure the work in place, so the next contractor could price it. Confirm in writing which subcontractors were owed what, and whether direct agreements allowed the owner to keep them on site. Read the bond and parent guarantee wording for what triggers a call and by when notice must be given. Keep the design team engaged and the drawings current. None of these actions accuses anyone. Each one shortens the stopped period if the worst arrives.

7. Root cause

The root cause, from the owner's side, was treating the contractor's financial health as settled at award. Contracts were let on price and reputation, the protections assumed an ordinary default, and nobody owned the question, "Can this contractor pay its supply chain next quarter?" The company's own failure had many causes, set out in the inquiry. The owners' exposure had one: they did not monitor the counterparty they depended on most.

Roman's view: how the cost lands

Roman puts it in numbers, hypothetical and round. On a 50,000,000 dollar contract, a default at 60 percent complete leaves 20,000,000 dollars of contract value unspent. A replacement contractor, inheriting partly built work it did not build and cannot warrant, prices at a premium, say 25 percent, so 25,000,000 dollars. Add a year of delay at a hypothetical carry of 300,000 dollars a month, 3,600,000 dollars, plus re-procurement, security and rectification. The owner now needs perhaps 30,000,000 dollars to finish what 20,000,000 dollars was meant to buy. A performance bond, retainage and parent guarantee are what stand between that gap and the owner's equity. Their size was set on the day of award, when the risk looked smallest.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, on default, termination and step-in rights; surety or insurance broker, on bond and guarantee cover.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming that the contractor's failure is the contractor's problem. On your project, it is yours, because you own the half-built building. The control is counterparty monitoring from award: named indicators, quarterly financial information where the contract allows it, a subcontractor payment check each month and a written step-in plan.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing the biggest name on the bid list and stopping there. Reputation is an input to prequalification, not a substitute for watching cash.

Callback

In Week 80, Roman treated Carillion as a single point of failure in a risk register and taught N-1 thinking from grid operations: plan for the loss of your largest asset. This week sees the same collapse from inside one project, where N-1 means a written answer to the question, "If this contractor stopped tomorrow, what would we do by Friday?"

Recap

Carillion issued a profit warning in July 2017 and was liquidated on January 15, 2018, leaving hospitals and other projects unfinished. The signs were cash signs, visible in its supply chain. Owners who depended on it had sized their protections for an ordinary default and monitored nothing.

Rule 121: Never let a contractor's size stand in for evidence of its solvency; monitor how it pays its subcontractors, how much of its revenue rests on unagreed claims and how it finances its supply chain, and keep a written step-in plan from the day of award.

Next: Roman on The Money: what each of the three failure modes costs, and who ends up paying.
checklist: I check how the contractor pays its subcontractors every month, not only at award.
I require financial information during the contract where the contract allows it.
I ask how much of the contractor's revenue rests on claims not yet agreed.
I treat long payment terms and supply-chain finance schemes as risk indicators.
I size bonds, retainage and parent guarantees for a total default, not an ordinary one.
I keep a written step-in plan from the day of award.
I document the state of the work monthly so a replacement can price it quickly.
I name one person who owns the contractor's financial risk.
head: Field checklist
speak: Carillion was one of the largest construction and services groups in the United Kingdom. It issued a profit warning in July 2017, driven by write-downs on construction contracts, and went into compulsory liquidation on January 15, 2018, leaving projects including two large hospitals to be finished by others, years late. The warning signs were cash signs: long payment terms pushed onto subcontractors, revenue resting on claims not yet agreed, a large pension deficit and dividends maintained while debt rose. From the owner's side, the root cause was treating the contractor's financial health as settled at award, with protections sized for an ordinary default. Roman's hypothetical numbers show why that matters: a default at 60 percent complete can turn 20 million dollars of remaining work into 30 million. Rule 121: never let size stand in for solvency; monitor payment practice and keep a step-in plan.
terms: Profit warning — a public statement by a listed company that its results will fall materially short of expectations.
Compulsory liquidation — a court-ordered winding up of an insolvent company, with its assets realised for creditors.
Step-in plan — an owner's prepared plan for taking control of a project and its supply chain if the main contractor fails.

hostile.q: Your contractor is a national firm with a strong name. Why are you asking for quarterly financials and checking how it pays its subcontractors?
hostile.a: Because size is not solvency, and the largest contractor in a country has failed before with hospitals half built. I am not alleging anything. I am monitoring the counterparty my whole project depends on, using the indicators that showed trouble first last time: how the supply chain is paid, how much revenue rests on unagreed claims and how the firm finances its suppliers. If the indicators stay clean, the cost is an hour a month. If they move, I will have months to act instead of days.

rule: Rule 121: Never let a contractor's size stand in for evidence of its solvency; monitor how it pays its subcontractors, how much of its revenue rests on unagreed claims and how it finances its supply chain, and keep a written step-in plan from the day of award.

title: What Each Failure Costs, and Who Ends Up Paying
summary: Roman prices the three construction failure modes, a change after sign-off, a bypassed hold point and a contractor collapse, and shows how each one moves cost, schedule, interest and value. The lesson is that the owner pays first and recovers later, if at all, so the cheapest protection is the one bought before the failure.
body:
Every construction failure is paid for first by whoever holds the project's cash and the lender's covenants, which is the owner; recovery from others comes later, slowly and in part, so the economics always favour prevention.

Recall

Q. What should you ask a builder on a benchmark tour that tends to produce the most valuable answer?

A. What they would change if they built it again tomorrow, followed by silence while they think.

Q. What is a warranty in construction closeout?

A. A promise by the contractor or a manufacturer to repair or replace defective work or equipment for a stated period after completion, separate from the owner's wider rights for latent defects.

Q. What is a low break?

A. A concrete cylinder test result below the specified strength, which triggers an investigation by the engineer and possibly in-place testing of the structure.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a lender looks at construction failure through one lens: does the loan stay in balance and does the building finish? When something goes wrong on site, the cost to complete rises today, the interest reserve burns faster and the completion date moves, while any recovery from a contractor, designer, surety or insurer arrives months or years later. In between, you fund the gap. That timing is why I want you to price failures before they happen.

The four costs of any failure

Plain English first. Every failure costs you four ways. The direct cost: the rework, demolition, testing or replacement work. The time cost: every day the critical path moves, you pay site overheads and interest. The capital cost: the lender may stop draws, require more equity or tighten terms. And the value cost: a building with a known defect or a gap in its records is worth less to a buyer or lender at the end.

The professional framing is expected cost: probability times impact, summed across the ways something can go wrong. Week 80 taught you the risk register. Here the point is narrower: the impact of a construction failure is almost always larger than the direct cost, because time and capital multiply it.

Pricing the three failure modes

Worked example one, hypothetical, a change after sign-off. A structural connection is altered in a shop drawing without the engineer's review, and the error is found when cracking appears during construction, not after occupancy. Direct cost: investigation 60,000 dollars, a strengthening design 40,000 and retrofit work 300,000, total 400,000 dollars. Time cost: 2 months on the critical path at a carry of 200,000 dollars a month for interest and site overheads, 400,000 dollars. Capital cost: the lender's monitor requires an independent structural review before the next draw, 50,000 dollars and a 3-week pause. Total about 850,000 dollars, against the 5,000 dollars an engineer's review would have cost at the shop drawing stage. That is a ratio of roughly 170 to 1.

Worked example two, hypothetical, a bypassed hold point. Waterproofing to a basement wall is backfilled before inspection. A year after occupancy, water appears in a parking level. Excavation, membrane repair and reinstatement cost 250,000 dollars, plus 80,000 dollars of lost parking income and tenant claims. Because the building is complete, the cost falls on the owner first, with recovery depending on the contract, the warranty and the evidence. The hold point would have cost one inspection visit and perhaps half a day of standby.

Say that out loud now.

The direct cost is the smallest cost. Time and capital multiply every failure.

Worked example three, hypothetical, a contractor collapse. A 20,000,000 dollar contract fails at 55 percent complete. Re-procurement takes 3 months. The replacement prices the remaining 9,000,000 dollars of work at a 25 percent premium, 11,250,000 dollars, because it inherits work it did not build. Add 3 months of standstill and 2 months of slower progress at 200,000 dollars a month, 1,000,000 dollars, plus security, rectification and fees of 500,000 dollars. The owner needs about 12,750,000 dollars to finish 9,000,000 dollars of work, a gap of 3,750,000 dollars, before any recovery from a bond or retainage.

Who ends up paying

In theory, the party at fault pays. In practice, the order of payment is the reverse of the order of fault. The owner pays immediately, because the lender requires the loan to stay in balance. The owner then claims against the contractor, whose liability may be limited by contract and whose solvency may be the problem. Next comes the surety, if there is a bond, subject to the bond's terms and notice requirements. Then insurers, subject to policy wording and exclusions; defective workmanship itself is commonly excluded from many construction policies. Recovery is uncertain in amount and slow in time, and the legal cost of pursuing it is real.

Put the third example through that sequence. Retainage held at 10 percent on 11,000,000 dollars of billing is 1,100,000 dollars, available at once if the contract lets you apply it to completion costs. That leaves 2,650,000 dollars. A performance bond may cover much of it, but sureties investigate before they pay, commonly have options to complete, finance or pay, and can dispute the amount, so assume months, not weeks. In the meantime the lender wants the gap deposited before the next draw. The owner's real need is not the 3,750,000 dollar loss. It is about 2,650,000 dollars of liquidity, now, for an unknown period. That is the number to plan for.

How the best do it

The most disciplined institutional owners treat contractor failure and quality failure as budgeted risks, not surprises. They require, where they can, financial reporting from the contractor during the contract, run a monthly check with key subcontractors on whether they are being paid, hold retainage until defined milestones, and sometimes use joint cheques or direct payment arrangements for critical trades when warning signs appear. On quality, they fund independent inspection of the hold points that matter most rather than relying on the contractor's own quality control. A small developer can copy all of it: a monthly subcontractor payment call, an inspection budget line for the hold points you choose, and protections sized to a total default.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

For your personal balance sheet, the question is where a construction failure lands if the project cannot absorb it. If you have signed a cost-overrun or completion guarantee, it lands on you, at the moment you are least liquid. Record your guarantees as contingent liabilities, and ask whether your liquidity floor survives the largest plausible failure on your largest project, the 3,750,000 dollar gap in example three, for instance, at a scale that fits your own projects. If it does not, the answer is not optimism. It is better protection, smaller exposure or a partner. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this for your own affairs.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on cost to complete after any failure; lawyer, on recovery rights against contractor, designer and surety.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is budgeting recovery as if it were cash. A claim against a failed contractor is an uncertain, slow asset. The control is to fund the cost to complete from committed sources first, and to treat any recovery as upside when it arrives.

The beginner's mistake

Comparing the direct cost of a fix with the saving from a shortcut and concluding the shortcut was worth the risk. Add the time, capital and value costs before you compare.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya and Roman showed how an out-of-balance loan becomes a call on a personal guarantee. Every failure priced today flows into that same test. The in-balance calculation does not care whose fault the cost increase was; it only asks whether the money left will finish the building.

Recap

Every failure has four costs: direct, time, capital and value. Time and capital multiply the direct cost. The owner pays first and recovers later and in part. Price failure before it happens, budget inspection and monitoring, and never count recovery as cash.

Next: LEX on The Rules: the clauses that govern change, inspection and contractor insolvency, with a comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach the point.
checklist: I price every failure on four costs: direct, time, capital and value.
I compare a shortcut's saving with the full cost of failure, not the direct cost alone.
I fund cost to complete from committed sources and treat recoveries as upside.
I budget independent inspection for the hold points that matter most.
I check with key subcontractors every month whether they are being paid.
I size bonds and retainage for a total contractor default.
I record my guarantees as contingent liabilities and test my liquidity floor against them.
head: Field checklist
speak: Every construction failure is paid first by the owner, because the lender needs the loan in balance today, while recovery from the contractor, surety or insurer arrives later and in part. Each failure has four costs: the direct cost of rework, the time cost of overheads and interest while the critical path moves, the capital cost when the lender pauses draws, and the value cost of a building with a known defect. In a hypothetical shop-drawing change, a 5,000 dollar engineer's review would have avoided about 850,000 dollars. In a hypothetical contractor default at 55 percent, 9,000,000 dollars of remaining work cost about 12,750,000 to finish. The best owners treat these as budgeted risks: monthly subcontractor payment checks, retainage held to milestones and independent inspection of critical hold points. Never count a recovery as cash; it is slow and uncertain.
terms: Expected cost — the probability of a failure multiplied by its full impact, used to compare the cost of prevention with the cost of the risk.
Joint cheque — a payment made out jointly to the contractor and a subcontractor or supplier, so that money reaches the party doing the work.
Recovery — money later obtained from a contractor, designer, surety or insurer to offset a loss the owner has already funded.

hostile.q: You want to add 150,000 dollars to the budget for independent inspection and monitoring. The contractor already has quality control. Why pay twice?
hostile.a: Because the contractor's quality control works for the contractor, and the failures that hurt owners most are the ones made under the contractor's own schedule pressure. The 150,000 dollars covers independent release of the hold points that become invisible once covered, such as reinforcement on transfer slabs, below-grade waterproofing and fire-stopping, plus a monthly check on subcontractor payment. One avoided failure of the kind we priced pays for it several times over, and the inspection records also support the building's value at exit.

title: The Clauses That Govern Change, Inspection and Insolvency
summary: LEX explains how construction contracts typically handle changes after sign-off, inspections and the right to uncover work, and what happens when a contractor becomes insolvent, including why a clause allowing termination for insolvency may not work as written. Two Systems compares how Canada and Guyana approach the point.
body:
The contract decides who may change the design, who may cover work before it is inspected and what you may do when your contractor becomes insolvent, and in each case the words you signed matter more than what anyone said on site.

Recall

Q. What does normalising a benchmark cost mean?

A. Adjusting it for area basis, scope, date, location and quality so it can be compared with your own project, and writing down each adjustment.

Q. What is the difference between substantial and final completion, legally?

A. Substantial completion usually triggers occupancy, the start of warranty periods and often a release of part of the retainage. Final completion closes the contract and triggers the last payment. The exact consequences depend on the contract.

Q. Who should approve a change to formwork stripping times?

A. The engineer of record, on stated strength criteria, because stripping affects the structure's safety during construction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the three failure modes this week each have a legal mirror. A change after sign-off is a question of authority and of what a review stamp means. A bypassed hold point is a question of the contractor's duty to give notice and the owner's right to uncover. A contractor collapse is a question of termination, the bond and insolvency law. If you know where these live in your contract before anything goes wrong, you can act in hours instead of weeks.

Changes after sign-off: authority and the review stamp

Plain English first. Most construction contracts say that changes to the work are valid only when made in writing, by a change order or a written directive signed by someone with authority. Standard forms used in the United States, such as those published by the American Institute of Architects and ConsensusDocs, set out change procedures in detail. They also commonly provide that the designer's review of a shop drawing does not relieve the contractor of responsibility for deviations it has not specifically drawn to the designer's attention. That last point is why the contractor's submittal must flag a change clearly, and why the designer's stamp must say what was reviewed.

The professional framing: a substitution hidden in a shop drawing is not an approved change unless it was identified, reviewed and accepted in writing. Read your contract's actual provisions and the designer's review stamp wording, which differs between firms. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example one, hypothetical. A shop drawing shows a revised connection. The engineer's stamp reads "Reviewed for general conformance with design intent only." The contractor builds it. When a problem appears, the question is whether the contractor clearly identified the revision. If it did not, many standard forms would leave responsibility with the contractor. If it did and the engineer accepted it, responsibility shifts. Either way, the owner bears the delay first. The control is a contract requirement that every deviation be listed on a separate change request, never only drawn on a submittal.

Inspection, notice and the right to uncover

Contracts and specifications commonly require the contractor to give notice before covering work that is to be inspected. If the contractor covers it without that notice, it is commonly required to uncover and reinstate it at its own cost on request. If it gave notice and the owner asks for uncovering anyway, the cost usually depends on whether the work proves to be defective. In the United States, the building code also requires special inspections for certain work, performed by approved agencies and reported to the building official, independent of the contract. Verify the exact requirements against the current adopted edition and your contract wording.

Say that out loud now.

Covered without notice means uncovered at the contractor's cost, if my contract says so. I read it before the pour, not after.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A basement wall is backfilled before the waterproofing hold point is released. The owner directs uncovering. The contract requires 48 hours' notice before covering inspected work, and the contractor gave none. The contractor uncovers at its own cost. Had the owner's representative verbally told the site to "carry on" the day before, the contractor would argue waiver, the giving up of a right by conduct. That is why the owner's people must never release a hold point verbally.

Insolvency and termination

Many contracts let the owner terminate if the contractor becomes insolvent. Such clauses are often called ipso facto clauses, from the Latin for "by the fact itself". In the United States, federal bankruptcy law can restrict enforcement of a clause that terminates a contract solely because of a bankruptcy filing, and it brings an automatic stay, a pause on most actions against the debtor. In practice, owners often terminate instead for the contractor's actual failure to perform, after giving the notices the contract requires. The performance bond, if one exists, is a separate contract with the surety and has its own notice and claim conditions. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Worked example three, hypothetical. A contractor stops work and its subcontractors walk off. The owner wants to call the performance bond. The bond requires written notice declaring the contractor in default, a meeting offer to the surety within a stated period and the owner's continued performance of its own obligations, including payment of the balance due. The owner, angry, withholds the last progress payment and hires a replacement before telling the surety. The surety then argues that the owner has prejudiced its rights by taking away its option to complete. Whether that defence succeeds depends on the bond's wording and the law, but the owner has turned a clean claim into a dispute. The control is simple: read the bond before you act, and notify the surety first.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

Conceptually, Canada handles insolvency under federal law, through statutes for bankruptcy and for restructuring large companies, which generally restrict terminating a contract merely because a party is insolvent or has begun proceedings, subject to exceptions. Provinces regulate construction payment, typically through construction lien and, in several provinces, prompt payment legislation, including mandatory holdbacks, a percentage of each payment retained to protect those down the chain. Guyana's legal system rests on English common law with its own statutes; how its insolvency law treats termination on insolvency, and whether lien-style protections exist for construction, are questions for Guyanese counsel. Verify against primary source in both countries before relying on any of this.

Professional sign-off required: construction lawyer, on change, inspection, termination and bond provisions, in the governing jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is acting on what you believe the contract says during a crisis, terminating on insolvency alone, waiving a hold point verbally or accepting a change by silence. The control is a one-page contract map, prepared at award, listing the clauses on change, notice before covering, uncovering, termination and the bond, with the notice periods and who must sign.

The beginner's mistake

Assuming that because the engineer "saw" a shop drawing, the change in it was approved. Approval is in the wording of the stamp and the contract, not in the fact that someone looked.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX and Marco taught precedence, notices and conditions precedent in the AIA, ConsensusDocs and FIDIC families. This week puts those clauses under load: each failure mode turns on a notice given or not given, and a condition met or not met, exactly as that lesson warned.

Recap

Changes need written authority, and a review stamp approves only what was clearly shown. Covering work without required notice usually means uncovering at the contractor's cost. A clause terminating on insolvency alone may not be enforceable, so owners usually rely on performance failure, proper notice and the bond. Canada and Guyana differ; verify in each.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: pricing a contractor default to completion, step by step.
checklist: I prepare a one-page contract map of change, notice, uncovering, termination and bond clauses at award.
I require every deviation on a separate written change request, never only on a submittal.
I read the designer's review stamp wording and know what it approves.
I never release a hold point verbally, and neither do my representatives.
I know the notice period required before work is covered.
I do not terminate on insolvency alone without counsel's advice.
I read the bond's notice and claim conditions before I need them.
I confirm insolvency and payment law with local counsel in each country.
head: Field checklist
speak: Each construction failure has a legal mirror. Changes are usually valid only in writing, signed with authority, and a designer's review of a shop drawing commonly does not approve a deviation the contractor did not clearly flag. So require every deviation on a separate change request. Contracts commonly require notice before covering inspected work, and work covered without notice is usually uncovered at the contractor's cost; a verbal carry-on from your own representative can hand the contractor a waiver argument. On insolvency, a clause terminating merely because of bankruptcy may be restricted by United States bankruptcy law, which also imposes an automatic stay, so owners usually terminate for failure to perform after proper notice and look to the performance bond. Canada handles insolvency federally and construction payment provincially; Guyana's position needs Guyanese counsel. Verify everything against the primary source.
terms: Ipso facto clause — a contract term allowing termination because a party becomes insolvent or enters insolvency proceedings.
Automatic stay — a pause, imposed when bankruptcy proceedings begin, on most actions by creditors against the debtor.
Waiver — giving up a contractual right, which can happen by conduct, such as allowing work to proceed without objection.

hostile.q: Your contractor has filed for bankruptcy protection. Why haven't you terminated the contract yet?
hostile.a: Because terminating purely on the filing may not be enforceable and could breach the automatic stay, which would hand the estate a claim against us. Counsel is reviewing the contract and the filing. In the meantime we have secured the site, documented the work in place, notified the surety in line with the bond's conditions and contacted key subcontractors about continuing directly. If the contractor fails to perform, we will terminate on that ground with the required notices. I would rather lose two weeks than lose the termination.

title: Pricing a Contractor Default to Completion, Step by Step
summary: Quincy works a hypothetical contractor default from the last pay application to the owner's funding gap: verified work in place, overbilling, the true remaining scope, the replacement premium, delay and rectification, then the sources that close the gap. The method turns a shock into a number you can take to a lender.
body:
When a contractor fails, the first number that matters is not what you have paid but what it will cost to finish, measured from verified work in place; everything else follows from that one honest starting point.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between a hold point and a witness point?

A. At a hold point the work may not proceed until a named inspection is released in writing. At a witness point the inspector is notified and may attend, but work may proceed if they do not.

Q. What is a final punch list walk for?

A. To confirm that every item recorded at substantial completion has been closed, so that final completion can be certified and the last payment released.

Q. What is formwork?

A. The temporary mould, with its supports, that holds fresh concrete in shape until it can carry itself.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the day a contractor stops, everyone will give you numbers: the contractor's last application, the lender's undisbursed balance, the surety's first position. None of them answers your question. Your question is how much money, from where, by when, to finish the building. This is an odd-numbered week, so we work forward, step by step, from the facts on the day of default to the funding gap.

One discipline runs through the whole calculation. Every figure is either measured, contracted or assumed, and you label which. Measured figures come from your quantity surveyor and the monitor. Contracted figures come from the contract and the bond. Assumed figures, the premium, the delay and the subcontractor settlement, are your judgment, and they are where the range comes from.

The facts on the day of default

All figures are hypothetical and round. The contract sum is 20,000,000 dollars. The contractor has billed 12,000,000 dollars. Retainage, a percentage of each payment held back until completion, is 10 percent, so the owner has paid 10,800,000 dollars and holds 1,200,000 dollars. The lender's monitor and your quantity surveyor have measured the work actually in place at 11,000,000 dollars. Subcontractors report 700,000 dollars unpaid by the contractor. A performance bond exists with a penal sum, its maximum amount, of 10,000,000 dollars.

Step by step: the cost to complete

Step 1, find the overbilling. Billed 12,000,000 less verified work 11,000,000 gives 1,000,000 dollars billed ahead of work. That money was largely paid out, less its share of retainage. It is the first sign the contractor was short of cash, and it means the work left is larger than the contractor's account suggested.

Step 2, find the true remaining scope at contract prices. Contract sum 20,000,000 less verified work 11,000,000 gives 9,000,000 dollars of work still to be done, at the original contract rates.

Step 3, apply the replacement premium. A replacement contractor inherits partly built work it did not build, cannot fully warrant and must survey before it prices. Assume its price for the remaining scope is 20 percent above the original rates: 9,000,000 times 1.20 gives 10,800,000 dollars.

Step 4, add rectification. The survey finds defective work in place needing correction: 400,000 dollars.

Step 5, add the gap costs. Site security, insurance and protection of the works while stopped: 150,000 dollars. Re-procurement, which means legal, cost consultant and design team fees to package and tender the remaining work: 250,000 dollars.

Step 6, add delay. The site is stopped 3 months and then runs 1 month slower while the new contractor mobilises, 4 months in total. At a hypothetical carry of 180,000 dollars a month for interest and the owner's overheads, that is 720,000 dollars.

Step 7, add the subcontractor exposure. If the 700,000 dollars owed to subcontractors will become liens on the property, or if you need those subcontractors back on site, you may have to pay some or all of it again. Assume you pay 500,000 dollars to secure the critical trades.

Total cost to complete: 10,800,000 plus 400,000 plus 150,000 plus 250,000 plus 720,000 plus 500,000, which is 12,820,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Start from verified work in place. Price the remaining scope at the replacement's rates, then add rectification, gap costs, delay and the supply chain.

Step by step: the sources and the gap

Step 8, the contract balance you still have. The unbilled balance of the contract is 20,000,000 less 12,000,000, so 8,000,000 dollars, plus the retainage held of 1,200,000 dollars, for 9,200,000 dollars of money that was always committed to finishing the work. Whether you may apply retainage to completion costs depends on the contract; assume here that you may.

Step 9, the gap. Cost to complete 12,820,000 less committed 9,200,000 leaves 3,620,000 dollars.

Step 10, the bond. The surety's obligation is capped at the penal sum of 10,000,000 dollars and is governed by the bond's terms. The 3,620,000 dollar excess is well within it, so if the claim is valid and properly made, the surety may fund it, or may choose to complete the work itself. But the surety will investigate, and some costs, such as your own delay costs, may be disputed under the bond wording. Assume for planning that 2,500,000 dollars is recovered and 1,120,000 dollars is disputed.

Step 11, the liquidity need. Until the surety pays, which may take months, the lender requires the loan to stay in balance, so you may need to deposit the full 3,620,000 dollars. Your planning numbers are therefore: a 3,620,000 dollar funding need now, an expected final loss of about 1,120,000 dollars, and a range around both.

Testing the range

The gap rests on three soft numbers, so move each one. If the replacement premium is 30 percent rather than 20, the remaining scope costs 11,700,000 dollars, 900,000 more, and the gap rises to 4,520,000 dollars. If the stoppage lasts 6 months rather than 3, delay adds 540,000 dollars, and the gap becomes 4,160,000. If you can keep the subcontractors without paying the arrears, because direct agreements already give you that right, the gap falls by 500,000 to 3,120,000. The premium moves the answer most, so the fact to establish first is a real price from at least two replacement contractors. Present the lender with the base case, the range and the one action that narrows it.

A second check: what front-loading did

Run one more figure. Had the owner paid only for verified work, 11,000,000 dollars, less 10 percent retainage, it would have paid 9,900,000 dollars instead of 10,800,000. The 900,000 dollars of overpayment is money that left the project into a failing company. It is not recoverable from the bond as a matter of course; it is a claim against an insolvent contractor. That is why Week 117 insisted that pay applications be checked against measured work, and why Week 40's Rule says draws never run ahead of verified work.

Professional sign-off required: quantity surveyor, on work in place and cost to complete; construction lawyer, on retainage, bond and lien rights.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is starting the calculation from the contractor's last pay application rather than from verified work in place, which understates the remaining scope by exactly the amount of the overbilling. The control is an independent measurement of work in place within days of the default, before anyone discusses money.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the bond's penal sum as cash available. It is a cap on the surety's liability, subject to the bond's conditions, not a fund you can draw on.

Callback

In Week 51, Quincy and Nadia taught cost-to-complete forecasting and earned value: the difference between what has been spent and what has been earned. A default is the moment that discipline is tested hardest. An owner who tracked earned value monthly already knows the true work in place; an owner who tracked only payments finds out from the replacement contractor.

Recap

From verified work of 11,000,000 dollars on a 20,000,000 dollar contract, the remaining 9,000,000 dollars of work cost about 12,820,000 dollars to finish once the replacement premium, rectification, gap costs, delay and subcontractors were added. Committed funds of 9,200,000 dollars left a 3,620,000 dollar gap, partly recoverable from the bond, but needed in cash now.

Next: Marco on The Room: the morning the contractor's subcontractors say they have not been paid.
checklist: I measure work in place independently within days of any default.
I calculate overbilling as billed less verified work.
I price the remaining scope at a replacement contractor's rates, not the original ones.
I add rectification, gap costs, re-procurement, delay and subcontractor exposure.
I count only committed money as a source: unbilled balance and usable retainage.
I treat the bond as a capped, conditional claim, not cash.
I plan the liquidity need separately from the expected final loss.
I have a quantity surveyor and a lawyer confirm the numbers before I show a lender.
head: Field checklist
speak: When a contractor fails, start from verified work in place, never the last pay application. In a hypothetical 20,000,000 dollar contract, the contractor billed 12,000,000 but only 11,000,000 of work was in place, so 1,000,000 was billed ahead. The true remaining scope is 9,000,000 at contract rates. A replacement prices it 20 percent higher, 10,800,000. Add 400,000 of rectification, 150,000 to protect the site, 250,000 to re-procure, 720,000 for four months of delay and 500,000 to secure unpaid subcontractors: 12,820,000 to finish. The committed sources are the 8,000,000 unbilled balance and 1,200,000 of retainage, 9,200,000, leaving a 3,620,000 gap. The bond may cover much of it after investigation, but the lender wants the gap funded now. Plan the liquidity need separately from the expected loss, and test the replacement premium first, because it moves the answer most.
terms: Penal sum — the maximum amount a surety can be liable for under a bond.
Overbilling — the amount a contractor has billed beyond the value of the work actually in place.
Replacement premium — the extra a new contractor charges to finish work it did not start, inspect from the beginning or fully warrant.

hostile.q: You have a 10,000,000 dollar bond. Why do you need an extra 3,600,000 dollars of equity from us?
hostile.a: Because the bond is a capped, conditional claim, not cash. The surety will investigate before it pays, may choose to complete the work itself, and may dispute some of our costs under the bond wording. Meanwhile the lender requires the loan to stay in balance before the next draw. So we need 3,620,000 dollars of liquidity now, of which we expect to recover around 2,500,000 dollars from the surety over the coming months. I am asking for a bridge, with the surety recovery assigned back to it, not for a permanent loss.

title: The Morning the Subcontractors Say They Have Not Been Paid
summary: A scene in the site office after three subcontractors tell the owner's representative they have not been paid for two months. Marco shows how to meet the contractor's principal, what to say and never to say, the question behind the question and how to leave with facts and a plan without triggering the collapse you fear.
body:
When subcontractors say they have not been paid, you are hearing the earliest reliable sign of a contractor in trouble; the meeting that follows must get facts, protect the job and keep your options open, without accusing anyone or promising anything.

Recall

Q. State Rule 121.

A. Never let a contractor's size stand in for evidence of its solvency; monitor how it pays its subcontractors, how much of its revenue rests on unagreed claims and how it finances its supply chain, and keep a written step-in plan from the day of award.

Q. Who should attend a commissioning kick-off?

A. The owner, the commissioning authority, the design team for the systems involved, the contractor and the key trade subcontractors, and the people who will operate the building.

Q. Why are curing conditions important for concrete?

A. Because concrete gains strength through hydration, which needs moisture and suitable temperature; poor curing leaves weaker, more permeable concrete, especially at the surface.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Ford taught that a contractor's collapse shows first in how it pays its supply chain. Today that sign arrives in your site office. How you handle the next two hours decides whether you have months to prepare or days. Handle it too softly and you learn the truth from a lien. Handle it too hard and you can push a struggling contractor over the edge and walk your own subcontractors off site.

The scene

A hypothetical mid-rise job, eight months in. Three subcontractors, electrical, drywall and plumbing, tell your owner's representative on the same day that they have not been paid for two months, although your last two payments to the contractor were made on time. You ask the contractor's principal, the owner of the contracting firm, to meet you at the site office at 10. You bring your representative and a notebook. You do not bring your lawyer into the room, but you call your lawyer before the meeting.

Lines to say

"We've paid applications 7 and 8 in full. Three of your subcontractors tell us they haven't been paid for those periods. I'd like to understand what's happening." Facts first, no adjectives.

"Can you show me the payments you've made to each subcontractor for those two applications?" A specific, reasonable request that most contracts support.

"Before the next application, we'll need lien waivers from each subcontractor for the work previously paid." Lien waivers, signed releases of a subcontractor's right to claim against the property for work already paid, are standard; asking for them is a control, not an accusation.

"What would help you get the supply chain current by the next application?" This invites a plan and tells you whether one exists.

Say that out loud now.

We have paid you. They say they have not been paid. Show me the payments, and give me waivers before the next application.

Lines never to say

"Are you going bust?" It forces a denial and may be repeated to your subcontractors, who will stop work.

"Don't worry, we'll pay the subs directly." A promise made before you have checked your contract, your lender's consent and the lien law can make you liable for the whole supply chain and breach your own contract.

"We're terminating." Not in this meeting. Termination is a legal process with notices; Day 4 showed how saying it early can cost you the termination.

"Just tell me it'll be fine." You are asking to be reassured, and you will be.

The question behind the question

When the principal says, "It's a timing issue, we're waiting on another client's payment," the question behind it is whether your money has been used to fund another project. That is a serious matter in many places, because construction payments can carry trust-like obligations under some statutes. Do not argue it in the room. Ask: "So applications 7 and 8 were used for other commitments?" and write down the answer. When he says, "My subs are exaggerating," the question behind it is whether he expects you to stop checking. Reply: "Then the waivers will be easy to get."

When to stay silent

After you ask to see the payments, stop talking. If the answer is a long explanation instead of a document, the silence makes that obvious to both of you. Stay silent too when he offers a reason you did not ask for. Volunteered explanations are often the most revealing thing said in such meetings.

Holding your state

You will feel two pulls: anger, because your money has gone somewhere else, and fear, because the job may stop. Both make you talk too much. Keep your voice level and your sentences short. Write numbers and dates down in front of him. If you need to steady yourself, do it before you walk in: a few slow breaths while parked, never while driving. If the meeting turns heated, say, "Let's pause. I'll write to you this afternoon with what we need." Leaving calmly with a written follow-up is a position of strength.

Worked example: what you leave with

Hypothetical. You leave with a written note: applications 7 and 8 paid, 1,600,000 dollars in total; subcontractors report about 600,000 dollars unpaid; principal attributes it to another client's delayed payment; payment evidence promised by Thursday; waivers required before application 9. That afternoon you write to him confirming those points, call your lawyer and lender's monitor, ask your quantity surveyor to measure work in place, read the bond's notice conditions and start the step-in file: subcontractor contacts, current drawings and the state of each trade. Nobody has been accused. Every option remains open.

A second example, hypothetical. On Thursday he sends evidence for 1,000,000 dollars of the 1,600,000 dollars, and the waivers cover two of three trades. You now have a measured gap of roughly 600,000 dollars and a trend. Your next step is a written request under the contract for a payment plan and, if it fails, the default notice process, with counsel.

Telling the lender, and when

Your loan agreement almost certainly requires you to tell the lender about events that could materially affect the project, and unpaid subcontractors leading to liens are exactly that. Tell the lender and its monitor early, in writing, with facts and your plan, not a conclusion. A lender who learns from you on Tuesday is a partner in the response. A lender who learns from a lien search on the next draw is an adversary checking whether you breached a covenant. The message is short: what was reported, what you have asked for, by when, and what you are preparing in case it is not provided. Ask the monitor to measure work in place at the next visit. The cost of that email is nothing. The cost of silence can be a frozen loan at the moment you need it most.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a single conversation that either reassures you falsely or frightens the supply chain off site. The control is a script built on facts, documents and waivers, followed the same day by a written confirmation and quiet preparation.

The beginner's mistake

Waiting for the next application to see if things improve. By then the liens may be filed and the cash may be gone. Act on the first credible report.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the hostile-question pattern: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and "I'll confirm by Friday." Today you are the one asking the hard questions, and the same discipline applies in reverse: ask one fact at a time, accept nothing without a document and put the deadline in writing.

Recap

State the facts, ask for payment evidence and waivers, and invite a plan. Never ask if he is going bust, never promise to pay subcontractors directly and never say "terminate" in the room. Hear the question behind "timing issue", stay silent after the request, write it up the same day and prepare quietly.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: Post-Mortem Four, with a Red Pen drill on a hold point release and a change directive.
checklist: I call my lawyer before the meeting, not after.
I open with paid applications and reported non-payment, without adjectives.
I ask for payment evidence for each subcontractor.
I require lien waivers before the next application.
I never promise to pay subcontractors directly before checking the contract, lender and law.
I never say terminate in the room.
I confirm everything in writing the same day.
I start the step-in file and measure work in place quietly.
head: Field checklist
speak: When three subcontractors say they have not been paid for two months while you have paid the contractor on time, you are hearing the earliest reliable sign of trouble. Meet the contractor's principal with facts: we paid applications 7 and 8, your subcontractors say they have not been paid, show me the payments to each one, and we need lien waivers before the next application. Ask what would help him get current. Never ask if he is going bust, never promise to pay subcontractors directly before checking your contract, lender and lien law, and never say terminate in the room. When he calls it a timing issue, ask whether your payments went to other commitments and write the answer down. Stay silent after you ask for documents. The same day, confirm in writing, call your lawyer and monitor, measure work in place, read the bond and start the step-in file.
terms: Lien waiver — a signed release by a subcontractor or supplier of its right to claim against the property for work already paid.
Principal — here, the owner or senior executive of the contracting firm, with authority to commit it.
Construction trust — a statutory rule in some places requiring money paid for a project to be held for those who supplied work to it.

hostile.q: Your contractor's subcontractors are threatening liens. Why didn't you just pay them directly and keep the job moving?
hostile.a: Because paying them directly before checking the contract, the lender's consent and the lien law could make us liable for the whole supply chain, duplicate payments we have already made and breach our own contract. What we did instead was require payment evidence and lien waivers, confirm the position in writing, notify the lender's monitor, measure work in place and read the bond. If the contractor cannot get current, counsel has a plan to protect title and keep the critical trades, under a documented arrangement, not a promise made in a site office.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 121 Review: Post-Mortem Four, Construction
summary: Kema reviews the construction post-mortem: changes after sign-off, bypassed hold points and contractor collapse, Carillion and Rule 121, the four costs of failure, the governing clauses, pricing a default and the meeting about unpaid subcontractors. The Red Pen drill marks up a hold point release and a change directive.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: buildings rarely fail for lack of a control; they fail when an existing control is skipped under pressure, and the owner pays first for every skip.

Recall

Q. In a contractor default, why is retainage valuable?

A. Because it is money already held, available at once if the contract allows it to be applied to completion costs, while bond and other recoveries take months.

Q. What does integrated systems testing prove at closeout?

A. That building systems work together under real sequences, for example that a fire alarm signal drives smoke control, elevator recall and door release correctly.

Q. Why must a pre-pour checklist be signed before the concrete arrives?

A. Because once concrete is placed, errors in reinforcement, cover or embedded items can usually be corrected only by investigation, strengthening or demolition.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a post-mortem is only useful if it changes what you do on Monday morning. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can walk a site and recognise the three quiet events that precede most construction disasters. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the three failure modes of this post-mortem and their common root.

Answer: A change after sign-off that skipped its designer, a hold point bypassed under schedule pressure, and a contractor failing in plain sight. The common root is a control that existed and was treated as optional under pressure.

Question 2. What happened at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City in 1981, in one sentence?

Answer: Two suspended walkways collapsed on July 17, 1981, killing 114 people, after a hanger rod connection was changed during shop drawing preparation without proper review, roughly doubling the load on one connection.

Question 3. State Rule 121.

Answer: Never let a contractor's size stand in for evidence of its solvency; monitor how it pays its subcontractors, how much of its revenue rests on unagreed claims and how it finances its supply chain, and keep a written step-in plan from the day of award.

Question 4. What are the four costs of any construction failure?

Answer: Direct cost, time cost, capital cost and value cost. Time and capital usually multiply the direct cost several times over.

Question 5. Why might a clause terminating a contract for insolvency alone not work as written?

Answer: Because insolvency law, including United States bankruptcy law, can restrict enforcement of a clause that terminates solely because of insolvency, and proceedings bring an automatic stay. Owners usually terminate for failure to perform, after proper notice, and claim on the bond. Verify against the primary source.

Question 6. After a contractor default, where does the cost-to-complete calculation start?

Answer: From independently verified work in place, never from the contractor's last pay application, because overbilling hides inside the application.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ford taught the three failure modes and their common root, using the Hyatt Regency as the change-after-sign-off case. Ford and Roman took Carillion through seven steps from the owner's side and wrote Rule 121. Roman priced each failure on four costs and showed that the owner pays first. LEX read the change, inspection, uncovering and insolvency clauses, with Canada and Guyana compared. Quincy priced a default from verified work in place to a funding gap. Marco ran the meeting after subcontractors reported non-payment.

The Red Pen

Read these two hypothetical site records and find the defects before reading on.

Site diary, Level 3 transfer slab. 07:40 inspector delayed, trucks on site. Spoke to engineer's office by phone, they said fine to proceed if the steel matches the drawings. Superintendent confirmed steel matches. Pour started 08:15. Hold point released verbally. Also agreed with contractor's project manager to substitute the specified anchors on the level 4 facade brackets with an equivalent product to save time; shop drawing to follow. Signed: owner's site representative.

The defects. First, the hold point was released verbally, by phone, by an unnamed person at the engineer's office, which is not a written release by the named inspector. Second, the condition "if the steel matches the drawings" was judged by the contractor's own superintendent, the party with the schedule pressure. Third, the transfer slab is exactly the kind of element where a bypassed inspection is most costly, and nothing records that the engineer of record will now require scanning or cores. Fourth, a substitution was agreed on site, before any shop drawing or design review, which is a change after sign-off routed around the engineer. Fifth, "equivalent product" is undefined and has not been accepted by the designer responsible. Sixth, the owner's representative has signed a record that may support a waiver argument by the contractor on both issues.

The corrected record would read: inspector delayed, pour held, trucks placed on standby at the owner's cost under the contract, inspection completed and released in writing at 11:10, pour started 11:30; substitution request received and sent to the engineer of record for written review, no change until accepted. It costs a morning and some standby charges. It keeps every right the owner has.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "How do construction projects actually go wrong, and what do you do about it?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Usually not through anything exotic. Three quiet events cause most of the damage: a design change after sign-off that never goes back to the engineer, an inspection that gets skipped because the concrete trucks are already there, and a contractor whose cash is failing while we keep paying it. The Hyatt Regency walkway collapse began with a changed connection detail; Carillion's failure showed first in how it paid its supply chain. Every one of these costs far more than its direct repair, because delay and the lender's response multiply it, and we as owner pay first. So we keep a hold point register with named releasers, route every change to the responsible designer in writing, check monthly that subcontractors are being paid, size our bonds for a total default and keep a step-in plan from award. Waiting costs us standby. Skipping costs us the project."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you name all three failure modes? Did you give one real case for at least one of them? Did you say who pays first? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is your own people becoming the route around your controls: a representative who releases a hold point by phone, or agrees a substitution to keep the peace. The control is to name, in writing, who may release and who may approve, and to tell your team that you will always back them for waiting and never for skipping.

The beginner's mistake

Studying failures as stories about other people. Each case this week is a description of a morning on your own site, with different names.

Callback

In Week 2, Ford and Kema taught the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed, then ask why. Post-Mortem Four gives you three ready-made answers for every building you will ever build. Run them at your next pre-mortem by name: where could a change skip its designer, where could a hold point be bypassed, and how would we know our contractor was running short of cash?

Recap

Changes after sign-off, bypassed hold points and contractor collapse share one root: a skipped control. The owner pays first, so prevention is cheap and recovery is slow. Read the clauses before the crisis, price defaults from verified work and act on the first credible report of non-payment. Rule 121 keeps size from standing in for solvency.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was the construction post-mortem. Three quiet events cause most of the damage: a change after sign-off that skips its engineer, as at the Hyatt Regency in 1981; a hold point bypassed because the concrete trucks are already on site; and a contractor failing in plain sight, as Carillion did before its liquidation in January 2018. The common root is a control that existed and was treated as optional. Every failure has four costs, direct, time, capital and value, and the owner pays first while recoveries arrive slowly. The contract decides who may approve a change, what happens to work covered without notice and whether you can terminate for insolvency, which bankruptcy law may restrict. After a default, start from verified work in place. When subcontractors report non-payment, ask for evidence and waivers, confirm in writing and prepare quietly. Rule 121: never let size stand in for solvency.
terms: Post-mortem — a structured review of a failure to find its causes and the rule that would have prevented it.
Substitution — the replacement of a specified product or detail with another, which counts as a change requiring the designer's review.
Standby — the cost of keeping labour or equipment, such as concrete trucks, waiting, usually payable under the contract when the owner causes the wait.

hostile.q: Your site diary says the engineer's office said fine to proceed by phone. Isn't that good enough?
hostile.a: No. A hold point is released in writing by the named inspector, not by phone by an unnamed person, and the condition was checked by the contractor's own superintendent. We have told the engineer of record what happened, and the engineer is specifying a scan and cores for that slab before it carries load. We have also withdrawn the anchor substitution agreed on site; it goes to the engineer for written review. From today only the named inspector can release a hold point, and my representatives will be backed for waiting, never for skipping.
